stem: Which two of these do NOT, by themselves, make a function component re-render? (Choose two.)

options.text: Calling its own state setter with a value that differs from the current one
options.why: A new state value (by Object.is) always schedules a render of that component.

options.text: Its parent component re-rendering
options.why: By default React re-renders every child of a component that renders, whether or not props changed.

options.text: A context value it reads with useContext changing
options.why: Context consumers re-render when the nearest Provider value changes, even if nothing between them renders.

options.text: Some other code mutating the props object it received
options.why: React does not observe objects. Without a state update somewhere, nothing tells React to render again.

options.text: Assigning a new value to `ref.current`
options.why: Refs are deliberately mutable boxes that React does not track; changing one never schedules a render.

explanation: Only three things start a render: the component's own state changing, its parent rendering, or a context it reads changing. Props are just the arguments of that render; changing them without a state update anywhere is invisible to React. Refs are explicitly outside the render cycle, which is why they suit values that should not affect output.

stem: In which phase does React actually change the DOM?

options.text: The render phase, while it is calling your component functions
options.why: Rendering only calculates the next UI. It must stay free of side effects, including DOM writes.

options.text: The commit phase, after rendering has finished
options.why: React applies the minimal set of DOM changes in one go once the new tree has been computed.

options.text: The passive-effect phase, when useEffect callbacks run
options.why: Effects run after the DOM has already been updated; they are for synchronising with outside systems.

options.text: The scheduling phase, the moment setState is called
options.why: setState only queues an update. React decides later when to render and commit it.

explanation: A React update has three steps: trigger (a state change queues work), render (React calls components and diffs the result against the previous tree) and commit (React mutates the DOM, attaches refs and then runs effects). Keeping DOM writes in the commit phase is what lets React pause or discard renders safely.

stem: Keys passed to list items must be unique across the whole application, not just among the items of one list.

options.text: True
options.why: Keys are only compared among siblings in the same array, so uniqueness elsewhere does not matter.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: keys only need to be unique among siblings. Two different lists can reuse the same keys.

explanation: React uses keys to match children of one parent between renders. It never compares keys across different parents, so the same key in two separate lists is fine. Within one list, duplicate keys make React warn and can mix up item state.

stem: StrictMode's double rendering and double effect execution happen only in development builds, not in production.

options.text: True
options.why: Correct: StrictMode checks are development-only and are stripped from production builds.

options.text: False
options.why: Production builds render once and run each effect once; the extra calls exist only to surface impure code during development.

explanation: In development, StrictMode calls component bodies, initialisers and reducers twice and runs an extra setup–cleanup–setup cycle for effects. This helps you find impure renders and missing cleanups. None of it happens in production, so it never affects real users.

stem: Type the name of the special prop that React uses to match items in a rendered list between renders.
explanation: The `key` prop gives each sibling a stable identity. React uses it, not the item's position, to decide which existing component and DOM node an item in the new list corresponds to. It is not passed to the component as a prop.

stem: A user clicks a button whose handler calls `setCount(count + 1)`. Put what React does next in order.

options.text: React commits the changes to the DOM
The event handler runs and queues the state update
React runs the useEffect callbacks of the updated components
React calls the component function again with the new state
React compares the new output with the previous render

explanation: The handler queues the update (trigger). React then renders: it calls the component with the new state and reconciles the result against the previous tree. Next it commits the minimal DOM changes. Passive effects run last, after the commit.

stem: A parent component re-renders because its own state changed. It renders `<Child />`, which takes no props and has no state of its own. What happens to Child by default?

options.text: Nothing, because Child has no props that could have changed
options.why: React does not check props by default. Skipping unchanged children is opt-in through memo.

options.text: Child re-renders as well, even though nothing it uses has changed
options.why: Rendering is recursive: when a component renders, React renders everything it returns.

options.text: Child is unmounted and mounted again with fresh state
options.why: Re-rendering is not remounting. The same type at the same position keeps its state and DOM.

options.text: Child re-renders only if it reads a context that the parent provides
options.why: Context is one extra trigger; it is not a requirement for a child to re-render.

explanation: By default React re-renders the whole subtree under a component that renders. That is usually cheap, because rendering only produces a description and the commit touches the DOM only where output differs. When it is too expensive you can opt out with `memo`, or by passing elements in as `children` from a component that did not render.

options.text: render Parent, effect Parent, render A, effect A, render B, effect B
options.why: React renders the whole tree before committing, so no effect runs between renders.

options.text: render Parent, render A, render B, effect A, effect B, effect Parent
options.why: Renders go top-down; effects run after the commit, children before their parent.

options.text: render Parent, render A, render B, effect Parent, effect A, effect B (top-down)
options.why: Effects are not run top-down. A parent's effect runs after its children's effects.

options.text: render A, render B, render Parent, effect A, effect B, effect Parent
options.why: A parent must render first; its return value is what tells React to render the children.

explanation: Rendering is depth-first from the top: Parent, then A, then B. After the commit, React runs effects in the same order it finishes components, which is children before parents (A, B, then Parent). That way a parent's effect can rely on its children's effects having already run.

options.text: `B0`, because a different JSX branch creates a new component
options.why: React does not track which branch produced an element; it only compares type and position.
Same component type at the same position, so React keeps the state and only updates the label prop.

options.text: `A3`, because the label prop is ignored after the first render
options.why: Props are read on every render. Only the state survives; the label updates to B.

options.text: `B0` plus a warning asking for keys on conditional branches
options.why: React gives no such warning. If you want a reset here, adding different keys is how you ask for it.

explanation: Reconciliation compares the element type at each position in the tree. Both branches put a `Counter` in the first child slot of the `div`, so React treats it as the same component: state (3) is preserved and the new `label` prop is applied. To reset state between branches, give them different keys, for example `key="A"` and `key="B"`.

options.text: 2, because Counter itself is the same component in both branches
options.why: State survives only if every ancestor at that position also keeps its type.

options.text: 2, but its DOM node is recreated inside the new section
options.why: React cannot move state between subtrees; a remounted subtree starts with fresh state.

options.text: 0, because the new parent type remounts the whole subtree
options.why: A different element type at a position destroys that subtree, including all component state inside it.

options.text: 0, but only in development; production builds keep the value
options.why: The rule is the same in every build; it is how reconciliation works, not a development check.

explanation: When the element type at a position changes (here `div` to `section`), React does not try to diff the children. It unmounts the old subtree, with all its state and DOM, and mounts the new one. So the Counter starts again at 0. Keep wrapper types stable, or move the conditional styling into props, if the state must survive.

stem: A list renders `items.map(item => <Row key={Math.random()} item={item} />)`. Which two consequences follow? (Choose two.)

options.text: Every render gives each row a new key, so React unmounts and remounts every row
options.why: Keys that change on every render never match the previous ones, so no row is ever reused.

options.text: Each row loses its state and DOM, so an input inside it loses focus and typed text
options.why: Remounting creates fresh component state and new DOM nodes on every render.

options.text: React detects keys that change between renders and logs a development warning
options.why: React only warns about missing or duplicate keys. Unstable keys are silently accepted.

options.text: Nothing changes, because React generates each key once and caches it per item
options.why: React has no way to tie a random number to an item; the expression runs again on every render.

options.text: It is the recommended choice when items have no id of their own
options.why: Generate a stable id when the data is created instead, or use a natural unique field.

explanation: A key must be stable across renders as well as unique among siblings. A random key is unique but unstable, so on every render React sees all-new keys, throws away every row and builds them again. That is slow and destroys row state, focus and uncontrolled input values. Give items stable ids when they are created.

stem: A page renders `<ProfileForm key={userId} userId={userId} />`. The user switches from user u1 to user u2. Which two things happen? (Choose two.)

options.text: All state inside ProfileForm, including half-typed drafts, starts again from its initial values
options.why: A new key tells React this is a different component instance, so its state is created fresh.

options.text: ProfileForm's effects clean up and then run again, as on a real unmount and mount
options.why: Changing the key unmounts the old instance and mounts a new one, so effects go through cleanup and setup.

options.text: React reuses the existing DOM nodes and only updates the changed text
options.why: The old instance's DOM is discarded with it; the new instance creates its own nodes.

options.text: ProfileForm skips rendering when userId is unchanged, like memo
options.why: A key is not a memoisation hint. With the same key, ProfileForm still re-renders whenever its parent does.

options.text: React logs a warning because keys are meant only for list items
options.why: Keys work on any element. Using them to reset a component is a documented pattern.

explanation: A key is part of a component's identity. Changing it makes React unmount the old instance and mount a new one in its place: state resets, effects re-run and DOM is rebuilt. This is the cleanest way to reset a form when the entity it edits changes, instead of syncing state with an effect.

options.text: render, effect
options.why: That is the production output. In development StrictMode adds extra calls.

options.text: render, render, effect, effect (no cleanup in between)
options.why: StrictMode runs the cleanup between the two effect runs, simulating an unmount.

options.text: render, render, effect, cleanup, effect
options.why: Development StrictMode renders twice, then runs setup, a simulated cleanup, and setup again.

options.text: render, effect, cleanup, render, effect
options.why: The simulated remount does not render again; it only re-runs effects with the same state.

explanation: In development StrictMode calls each component body twice to expose impure rendering. After mounting, it also runs every effect's setup, then its cleanup, then setup again, to expose missing cleanups. React 19 does not hide the second render's logs (DevTools dims them). Production runs each once.

stem: In React 19, `ReactDOM.render(<App />, container)` still works but logs a deprecation warning.

options.text: True
options.why: It no longer works in React 19: `ReactDOM.render` was removed, not just deprecated.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: React 19 removed `ReactDOM.render` (and `hydrate`). Use `createRoot(container).render(<App />)`.

explanation: React 18 deprecated the legacy root API, and React 19 removed `ReactDOM.render`, `ReactDOM.hydrate`, `unmountComponentAtNode` and `findDOMNode` from `react-dom`. Apps must use `createRoot` or `hydrateRoot` from `react-dom/client`, which also enable concurrent features.

options.text: onClick needs a string handler name, as in HTML attributes
options.why: React expects a function value for onClick, not a string.

options.text: The setter runs during render, which causes an endless render loop
options.why: React stops the loop and throws "Too many re-renders".

options.text: State setters cannot be passed to event props without useCallback
options.why: Setters are stable functions and can be passed directly; useCallback is never required.

options.text: The button renders, but every click adds 2 because of batching
options.why: The handler is never a function here; the setter is called during render, not on click.

explanation: The braces evaluate `setCount(count + 1)` while rendering and pass its return value (undefined) as the handler. Setting state during render queues another render, which sets state again, and so on. React detects the loop and throws "Too many re-renders. React limits the number of renders to prevent an infinite loop." Pass a function instead: `onClick={() => setCount(count + 1)}`.

stem: Match each change with what happens to the state of a `<Counter />` rendered by it.

options.text: Counter keeps its state
Counter remounts and its state resets
Counter does not render at all
React throws an error

prompts.text: The parent passes Counter a different `label` prop at the same position
The parent wraps Counter in a `<section>` instead of a `<div>`
Counter calls `setN(5)` when n is already 5, after React has already bailed out once
Counter calls its own setter unconditionally in its function body

explanation: Same type at the same position keeps state; a different ancestor type remounts the subtree. Setting state to an Object.is-equal value lets React bail out without rendering. Unconditional setState during render loops until React throws "Too many re-renders".

stem: Match each piece of code with when React runs it during a mount.

options.text: During render, before any DOM change
During commit, as soon as its DOM node is attached
After DOM mutations, before the browser paints
After the commit, normally after the browser has painted

explanation: Component bodies run in the render phase. During commit React mutates the DOM and attaches refs (callback refs are called then), and runs layout effects synchronously so they can measure before paint. Passive effects from useEffect are flushed afterwards, usually after paint. For updates caused by discrete events such as clicks, React may flush them before paint.

stem: Each item needs to render a `<dt>` and a `<dd>` with no wrapper element. Which version is correct?

options.text: `items.map(i => <><dt>{i.term}</dt><dd>{i.desc}</dd></>)`
options.why: The shorthand fragment cannot take a key, so React warns that list children need keys.

options.text: `items.map(i => < key={i.id}><dt>{i.term}</dt><dd>{i.desc}</dd></>)`
options.why: That is not valid JSX. The empty-tag shorthand accepts no attributes at all.

options.text: `items.map(i => <Fragment key={i.id}><dt>{i.term}</dt><dd>{i.desc}</dd></Fragment>)`
options.why: The explicit Fragment accepts a key and still adds no DOM element.

options.text: `items.map(i => [<dt>{i.term}</dt>, <dd>{i.desc}</dd>])`, with no keys on the elements
options.why: Nested arrays still need keys on their elements, so React warns about every pair.

explanation: Keys belong on the outermost element returned from `map`. When that element is a fragment, use the explicit `<Fragment key={...}>` form, because the `<>...</>` shorthand cannot carry props. Fragments add nothing to the DOM, which keeps `<dl>` markup valid.

options.text: Banana: b-note and Cherry: c-note
options.why: That is what stable `key={it.id}` would give: each input would stay with its item.

options.text: Banana: a-note and Cherry: b-note
options.why: Keys 0 and 1 survive, so their inputs (a-note, b-note) stay; key 2 and its c-note are removed.

options.text: Banana: (empty) and Cherry: (empty), because the list re-renders
options.why: Re-rendering does not clear uncontrolled inputs; only unmounting does.

options.text: Apple: a-note and Banana: b-note, because the deleted row is re-added
options.why: The text comes from the new data, so Apple is gone; only the DOM inputs are mismatched.

explanation: With index keys, React matches rows by position. After the deletion the new list has keys 0 and 1, which React maps to the old rows 0 and 1, so those DOM nodes, including the typed text, are kept and only their labels change. The old row with key 2 (holding "c-note") is unmounted. Text and data are now misaligned. Keying by `it.id` fixes it.

options.why: That would require keys tied to the names; index keys tie state to positions instead.
Key 0 kept its state (2) but now receives name "a"; keys 1 and 2 hold fresh or shifted state.

options.why: Only the newly added key (2) mounts; keys 0 and 1 are reused.

options.text: `a=2 b=2 c=0`, because state is copied to the new row
options.why: React never copies state between instances; each key has exactly one instance.

explanation: Index keys bind state to positions. Before: key 0 → b (n=2), key 1 → c (n=0). After prepending, key 0 renders "a" with the old n=2, key 1 renders "b" with c's old n=0, and key 2 is new for "c" with n=0. The count has visibly jumped to a different item. Use stable keys such as the name or an id.

So the div always has two child slots and Counter is always in the second: state survives. Compare this with code that returns structurally different trees, where positions do shift.

This looks like the `&&` version but behaves differently. Here the hidden case returns a div with one child, so Counter is child 0. When shown, child 0 is a `

Declaring `Inner` inside `Outer` creates a new function on every render, so React sees a different component type each time and remounts it, losing state and DOM. Top did not render again, so the element is the identical object, and React bails out of rendering it. Passing components down as children is a cheap way to keep them out of a stateful wrapper's renders.

The mutation is also dangerous: the previous render's data was modified. Create a new array instead: `setItems([...items, items.length + 1])`, or the functional form.

StrictMode in development calls state initialiser functions twice (as well as component bodies and reducers), using one result and discarding the other, to expose impurity. So "init" is logged twice in development and once in production. Initialisers must be pure; reading local storage is fine, but side effects such as analytics calls are not.

Server HTML contains `

time 1

`, but the first client render produces `

time 2

` (no suppressHydrationWarning). In React 19, what happens? (Choose two.)

options.text: React reports a recoverable hydration error, for example through onRecoverableError
options.why: React 19 surfaces mismatches as recoverable errors with a diff in development.

options.text: React discards the server HTML for that tree and renders it on the client, so the DOM ends up showing "time 2"
options.why: Instead of patching mismatches, React regenerates the affected tree from client output.

options.text: React silently keeps "time 1" in the DOM until the next state update
options.why: Keeping the server text without an error only happens when suppressHydrationWarning is set.

options.text: React patches just the one text node and logs nothing
options.why: Quiet text patching was React 16 behaviour; modern React treats mismatches as errors.

options.text: Hydration stops and the page stays without event handlers
options.why: Hydration recovers by client rendering; the page still becomes interactive.

explanation: From React 18 on, a hydration mismatch is a recoverable error. React throws away the server-rendered DOM for the nearest boundary (the root if there is no Suspense boundary) and renders it on the client, then reports the error through `onRecoverableError` and the console. This costs performance and can cause a flash, so render the same output on both sides.

stem: Match each hydration situation with what React 19 does.

options.text: Hydrates by attaching handlers to the existing DOM, with no errors
Regenerates the tree on the client and reports a recoverable error
Keeps the server text and reports nothing
Patches the text node quietly and logs a warning only

prompts.text: Server and client output are identical
A text node differs, and nothing suppresses the warning
A text node differs inside an element marked `suppressHydrationWarning`

explanation: Identical output hydrates silently. A mismatch without suppression makes React client-render that tree and report a recoverable error. `suppressHydrationWarning` on the element whose own text differs tells React to accept the difference: it keeps the server text and reports nothing until a later client update changes it. The quiet patch-and-warn option describes React 16, not React 19.

stem: React logs "Cannot update a component (`Parent`) while rendering a different component (`Child`)". Which code causes it?

options.text: Child calls `props.onSelect(id)` inside a click handler
options.why: Calling a parent's setter from an event handler is the normal way to lift state.

options.text: Child calls `props.onSelect(id)` directly in its function body
options.why: That sets Parent's state while Child is rendering, which React forbids.

options.text: Child calls `props.onSelect(id)` inside a useEffect
options.why: Effects run after the commit, so updating a parent there is allowed, if sometimes wasteful.

options.text: Child calls its own setter during render to adjust state from new props
options.why: Updating the component's own state during render is the supported derived-state pattern.

explanation: Rendering must be pure. A component may set its own state during render (React re-runs it right away), but it must not update another component while rendering. That is what the warning reports. Move the call into an event handler, or compute the value in the parent instead of reporting it up from the child's render.

stem: Parent P renders children A and B. Each of the three has `useEffect(() => { log("effect X"); return () => log("cleanup X"); }, [v])`. When `v` changes and all three re-render, put the logs in order.

options.text: effect A
cleanup P
cleanup A
effect P
cleanup B
effect B

explanation: On an update React first runs the cleanups of every effect whose dependencies changed, then all the new setups. Both passes go through the tree in the same child-before-parent order: cleanup A, cleanup B, cleanup P, then effect A, effect B, effect P. No new effect runs while an old one for the same commit is still set up.

stem: Which three of these lines are bugs when written directly in a component's body (not in an event handler or effect)? (Choose three.)

options.text: `props.items.sort((a, b) => a.price - b.price)`
options.why: sort mutates the array in place, which changes the parent's data during render.

options.text: `document.title = props.title`
options.why: Writing to the DOM is a side effect; it belongs in an effect, or in React 19 `<title>` rendering.

options.text: `props.onLoaded(data.length)` where onLoaded sets the parent's state
options.why: Updating another component during render triggers React's "Cannot update a component" warning.

options.text: `const sorted = [...props.items].sort(byPrice)`
options.why: Copying before sorting keeps render pure; only the local copy changes.

options.text: `const style = { color }; style.fontWeight = bold ? 700 : 400;`
options.why: Mutating an object created during this render is fine; nobody else can see it yet.

options.text: `const total = props.items.reduce((s, i) => s + i.price, 0)`
options.why: Deriving values from props during render is exactly what render is for.

explanation: Render must behave like a pure function of props, state and context: same inputs, same output, and no changes to anything that existed before the call. Mutating props, touching the DOM or updating other components breaks that and causes bugs under StrictMode and concurrent rendering. Local mutation of objects you just created is allowed.

stem: React can pause, interrupt or throw away a render, but it always performs the commit in one uninterrupted step. Why?

options.text: Commits are always so cheap that making them interruptible would not save any time
options.why: Cost is not the reason; consistency is.

options.text: Rendering builds an unseen tree in memory; the commit changes the visible DOM
options.why: Unseen work can be abandoned safely; a half-applied DOM update would show users an inconsistent UI.

options.text: The browser locks the DOM during a commit, so React cannot yield
options.why: Nothing in the DOM API forces this; React chooses to commit synchronously.

options.text: Commits run in a web worker, which cannot be interrupted
options.why: React renders and commits on the main thread; DOM APIs are not available in workers.

explanation: With the fiber architecture, rendering produces a work-in-progress tree that nobody can see, so React can split it into units, pause for higher-priority work, or throw it away and restart. The commit applies all DOM mutations, refs and layout effects for that render together, so the user never sees a partially updated screen.

options.text: Click 1: parent, child. Clicks 2 and 3: nothing
options.why: Plausible, but React may need one more render of Parent before it can bail out.

options.text: Click 1: parent, child. Click 2: parent. Click 3: nothing
options.why: The second click renders Parent once more and then bails out before its children; the third is skipped entirely.

options.text: Each click: parent, child
options.why: Setting state to the current value lets React bail out; it does not render the tree every time.

options.text: Click 1: parent, child. Clicks 2 and 3: parent (Child is skipped)
options.why: After the extra render confirms the value is unchanged, React can skip the third click without rendering.

explanation: If you set state to an Object.is-equal value, React bails out, but the docs warn it "may still need to call your component before skipping the children". Here the first click changes 0 to 1 (full render). The second sets 1 again: React has to render Parent once to confirm, then skips Child. On the third, it can tell up front that nothing changed and does not render at all. Never rely on render counts for logic.

explanation: When a subtree is deleted, React traverses it from the root of the deletion and calls each fiber's effect cleanups as it reaches it, so the parent comes first and siblings follow in order. That differs from updates, where cleanups and setups run child-first. Design cleanups so they don't depend on a sibling or parent still being mounted.

stem: Parent P renders A and B, each with a mount-only effect (`[]`) that logs on setup and cleanup. What does mounting log in development with StrictMode?

options.text: effect A, effect B, effect P, cleanup A, cleanup B, cleanup P, effect A, effect B, effect P
options.why: The simulated unmount uses the deletion order, which runs the parent's cleanup first.

options.text: effect A, effect B, effect P, cleanup P, cleanup A, cleanup B, effect A, effect B, effect P
options.why: Setup child-first, simulated unmount parent-first, then setup child-first again.

options.text: effect A, cleanup A, effect A, effect B, cleanup B, effect B, effect P, cleanup P, effect P
options.why: StrictMode replays the whole tree's effects together, not each component's effects back to back.

options.text: effect A, effect B, effect P, then the same three again, with no cleanups at all in between
options.why: The double invocation always includes the cleanups in between.

explanation: In development StrictMode mounts the tree, then simulates unmounting and remounting it. Setup runs in the usual child-before-parent order. The simulated unmount follows deletion order (parent first). Then setup runs child-first again. If your effects work only when this extra cycle is absent, they are missing a cleanup.

options.why: That would require a fresh ref for the second setup, but the simulated remount keeps state and refs.

options.why: StrictMode's remount is simulated: the same ref survives, so the counter keeps going.

options.text: effect 1, effect 2
options.why: StrictMode always runs the cleanup between the two setups.

options.text: effect 1
options.why: That is the production output; development StrictMode re-runs the effect.

explanation: StrictMode's extra cycle does not create a new instance. React runs the cleanup and the setup again on the same component, reusing its state and refs. So a ref-based "has mounted" guard does not reset: the ref reads 1 in the second setup and becomes 2. Code that tries to skip the second run with a ref usually hides a missing cleanup instead of fixing it.

stem: P renders child C. Both components call `useLayoutEffect(() => log("X layout"))` and `useEffect(() => log("X effect"))`, and P also logs "P render" in its body. Put the logs from mounting in order.

options.text: P layout
C effect
P render
C layout
P effect

explanation: Render happens first (P render, then C's render). During the commit, after the DOM is updated, React runs all layout effects child-first (C layout, P layout) synchronously. Passive effects are flushed after the commit, again child-first (C effect, P effect). Every layout effect in a commit runs before any passive effect of that commit.

stem: Rows use `key={index}` and contain uncontrolled inputs, so deleting a row leaves typed text in the wrong rows. Which two changes fix the bug? (Choose two.)

options.text: Key each row by a stable item id instead of the index
options.why: Each row's DOM and state then follow its item, so deleting an item removes its own input.

options.text: Make the inputs controlled, storing each value on its item and rendering `value={item.note}`
options.why: The value then lives in the data, so even if DOM nodes are reused they show the right item's text.

options.text: Wrap each row component in React.memo
options.why: memo only skips renders; it doesn't change how rows are matched by key.

options.text: Use `key={Math.random()}` so that every row is unique
options.why: Rows would remount on every render, so every input would lose its text on each keystroke.

options.text: Call `useId()` inside the map callback to make a key for each row
options.why: Hooks can't be called in loops or callbacks, and a new id per render would not be stable anyway.

explanation: The bug comes from tying DOM state to positions. Either give React a key that follows the data (a stable id), or keep the state in the data rather than in the DOM, so that position-based reuse still shows the right values. Stable ids are the better default, since they also keep focus, scroll position and component state with the right item.

Only Layout and Footer run. Layout owns the state, so it renders, and `<Footer />` is a new element created during that render. `sidebar` and `children` are element objects App created earlier; App did not render, so they are identical and React skips Sidebar and Content. Elements passed through props behave like any other stable value.

stem: A server-rendered page shows the time with `{new Date().toLocaleTimeString()}`, which causes a hydration mismatch. Which two approaches fix it correctly? (Choose two.)

options.text: Render a placeholder on the server and first client render, then set the real time in a useEffect
options.why: Both sides render the same initial output, and the client-only value appears after hydration.

options.text: Add `suppressHydrationWarning` to the span, accepting server text until the next client update
options.why: It is meant for this case: one element whose own text legitimately differs, such as a timestamp.

options.text: Add `suppressHydrationWarning` to a wrapper div around the whole clock component
options.why: It only works one level deep, on the element's own text and attributes, not on its descendants.

options.text: Compute the time inside useMemo so it is calculated only once
options.why: useMemo runs separately on server and client, so the values still differ.

options.text: Set the text in useLayoutEffect, which runs before hydration compares the markup
options.why: Layout effects run after hydration has matched the tree, so the mismatch has already happened.

explanation: Hydration requires the first client render to match the server HTML exactly. For values that differ by environment, either render the same placeholder first and update in an effect (two-pass rendering), or mark the one element whose content differs with `suppressHydrationWarning`. The suppression applies only to that element's own text and attributes, one level deep. Neither memoising nor layout effects change what the first render produces.
